Observe whether you can clearly document routes, segment identifiers, units, and test conditions, calculate given budgets, and identify exceeded limits without treating a passing table as real service recovery; then check practical conditions such as weather, attendance, and work qualifications.

Specific signs include willingness to check drawings and test records, checking objects and conditions first when values change, explaining which evidence supports conclusions and which services remain untested, and handing colleagues reviewable information.

Signs warranting caution include acting before checking sites, treating identical cable names as the same system, bypassing permission to meet deadlines, or treating one normal reading as full recovery. Observe behavior with paper materials first.

Afterward, retain G1/G2/G3 calculations and scope explanations, observing willingness to recheck units, revise conclusions, and explain unknowns; do not assign yourself courage or career talent scores.

The exact US identity is O*NET49-9052.00, installing and repairing telecommunications cables, including fiber optics. Tasks may include splicing, line testing, underground or overhead installation, customer access, and tool maintenance; electrical power transmission and distribution lines are a separate occupation. Check China against actual duties.

Inputs include line diagrams, work orders, cables and segment identifiers, site conditions, and existing test records. Check objects and permitted scope first; do not invent unknown addresses, underground facility locations, affected users, or work permissions.

For new lines, first check that diagram routes, cables, and segment identifiers correspond, then check materials, site conditions, and permitted scope, following applicable procedures for implementation, testing, and handover. Poles and towers, excavation, vehicles, and underground spaces require separate condition checks; this page offers paper checks only.

For maintenance, first check whether segment identifiers, units, and test conditions in existing records are comparable, then analyze readings and anomaly locations. Inconsistent conditions cannot be compared directly; even an anomaly does not allow one value to establish the exact damage cause or authorize opening cables yourself.

Retest lines after installation or repair as agreed, recording line, service, and unconfirmed items separately. Paper G2 changes only segment Y's budget input: the total changes from 2.9 to 3.3 dB, exceeding the limit by 0.3 and requiring withdrawal of the original budget pass; this change confirms neither causes nor real service status.

Collaborate with construction, service, and user-related personnel, explaining locations, conditions, measured data, and unresolved issues. Pause for hazards or unclear permissions and refer to authorized owners; emergencies do not justify expanding work yourself.

Cleaning and maintaining tools and test equipment and keeping line and facility records are also tasks. Handle splicing, terminals, and associated equipment according to actual arrangements; not everyone is responsible for network design.

Deliver route and splice records, test and fault explanations, retesting, and user-service explanations. Telecommunications line installers and repairers install, splice, and repair telecommunications cables, including optical fiber; inspect and analyze line test results, record maintenance and retesting, and explain services to users. Tasks may involve overhead, underground, or customer access work; electrical power transmission and distribution lines and equipment installation and repair are related but distinct occupational scopes.

Telecommunications equipment installers and repairers mainly set up, adjust, and repair switching, distribution, routing, and customer equipment, potentially including wiring. Their work overlaps with lines, but equipment status and service delivery require independent verification.

Electrical power-line installers and repairers handle transmission and distribution cables and associated facilities. Power risks and permissions differ; communication line experience cannot replace their training and work qualifications.

Radio, cellular, and tower equipment installers and repairers handle transmitters and receivers, two-way radio systems, and coverage testing. Check radio-frequency equipment and tower tasks separately; these are not optical cable maintenance.

Electricians install, maintain, and repair electrical wiring, equipment, and facilities, checking electrical systems against corresponding codes. Shared drawing-reading tasks do not mean communication line workers already have this work competence.

The historical Mile name-related announcement lacks detailed duties, pay components, gross versus net amounts, shifts, contracts, and a closing date; live vacancies were not rechecked this round. The exact US 2025 49-9052 annual median of $74,330 and that announcement's 2000–10000 yuan/month cannot replace one another. The planned 5 recruits are not five samples; amounts are not annualized or guaranteed take-home pay. In China's information transmission, software, and information technology services industry in 2025, urban-unit average annual gross wages were 248,752 yuan/year for non-private units and 128,166 yuan/year for private units. The two unit populations are measured separately and are not combined into a personal wage range. Coverage includes legal-entity units employing 5 or more people in urban areas, excludes individual businesses and freelancers, and includes personal income tax, social insurance, and housing provident fund deductions and contributions. These figures provide background only when the actual employer belongs to this industry; construction contracting, manufacturing, labor dispatch, and other industries are not automatically included based on line tasks or work locations. These are not telecommunications line installation and repair occupational median wages, starting pay, contracted project quotations, or net income after costs, and do not fill gaps in the exact national distribution or independent employer offers.
